data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms without smuggling in induction, provided one accepts that rational action requires choosing the theory with the highest 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) among unfalsified contenders, even though corroboration reports only past performance and guarantees nothing about the future. The cost of this solution is the abandonment of any claim that science converges toward truth with increasing probability; instead, science becomes a game of eliminating error where the 'best' theory is merely the one currently surviving the severest tests, not the one most likely to be true.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If it can be shown that preferring a theory solely on past survival implicitly assumes the uniformity of nature (that the future will resemble the past), then the preference is inductive after all.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' cannot be defined or assessed without relying on inductive generalizations from observed truths to unobserved ones, then the defense collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists actually act on the belief that better-corroborated theories are *more probable* to be true (rather than just less easily falsified), then Popper's description of scientific practice contradicts his own philosophy.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument distinguishes between 'logical probability' (which Popper rejects as applicable to universal laws) and 'rational preferability' based on critical scrutiny. It posits that while we cannot infer the future from the past (induction), we can rationally prefer the theory that has withstood more severe attempts at falsification because it contains more empirical content and has survived closer attempts to destroy it. This preference is a methodological rule for error elimination, not an inductive prediction of success.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
